name: Management Accounting
title: Controller
blurb: SAP CO is management accounting in software form, and cost, margin and break-even thinking is the backbone of every strategy-consulting case.

chapters.title: Cost behaviour, CVP and break-even
chapters.read: A management accounting textbook's chapters on fixed, variable and mixed costs (the high-low method), contribution margin and cost-volume-profit analysis, including target profit and margin of safety.
chapters.produce: Build a one-sheet CVP model for a ramen shop (price, variable cost per bowl, monthly fixed costs) that outputs break-even bowls, target-profit volume, margin of safety and a break-even chart.

quiz.q: A product sells for ¥2,000 with variable cost ¥1,200 per unit. Fixed costs are ¥400,000 per month. What is the break-even volume in units?
quiz.ex: Contribution per unit 800. 400,000 ÷ 800 = 500 units.

quiz.q: Same product (price ¥2,000, variable cost ¥1,200, fixed costs ¥400,000). How many units must be sold to earn a profit of ¥200,000?
Same product (price ¥2,000, variable cost ¥1,200). What is the contribution margin ratio?
Using the high-low method: in the lowest month 1,000 units were made at a total cost of ¥550,000; in the highest month 1,600 units cost ¥730,000. What is the estimated fixed cost per month?
Within the relevant range, what happens to fixed cost per unit as output rises?
opts: It turns into a variable cost
quiz.ex: Total fixed cost stays the same, so spreading it across more units lowers the cost per unit.

quiz.q: Actual sales are 800 units and break-even is 500 units. What is the margin of safety ratio?

chapters.title: Cost centres, profit centres and internal orders
chapters.read: A management accounting text's chapter on responsibility accounting, then SAP Learning (learning.sap.com) material on overhead cost controlling in S/4HANA: cost centres, cost elements, activity types, internal orders and settlement, and profit centres.
chapters.produce: Design a cost-centre and profit-centre hierarchy for a fictional 200-person manufacturer, with two service cost centres allocated by drivers you choose and one internal order for a trade fair settled to marketing.

quiz.q: A cost centre manager is normally held responsible for:
quiz.ex: A cost centre is accountable for controlling its costs; profit centres add revenue, and investment centres add capital employed.

quiz.q: In SAP CO, what is an internal order typically used for?
opts: Replacing general ledger accounts in FI
Collecting costs for a short-lived activity, such as a trade fair, and then settling them to a cost centre or other receiver
Representing a permanent department in the organisation
quiz.ex: Internal orders gather costs for a specific job or event over its life and then settle them to the receivers that should bear them.

quiz.q: The IT cost centre's costs of ¥900,000 are allocated by number of PCs: Production 30, Sales 15, Admin 15. How much is allocated to Sales?
A machine cost centre plans costs of ¥4,800,000 for 3,000 machine hours. What is the planned activity price per hour?
A business unit is evaluated on return on investment (ROI). What kind of responsibility centre is it?
quiz.ex: ROI relates profit to the capital invested, so the manager must control investment as well as revenue and cost.

quiz.q: Which statement about secondary cost elements in SAP CO is correct?
opts: They correspond one-to-one to the external expense accounts in the P&L
They are used only to post revenue
They are used for internal allocations such as assessments and activity allocations, not for recording external expenses
quiz.ex: Primary cost elements carry costs coming in from FI; secondary cost elements move costs between CO objects.

chapters.title: Product costing: job and process
chapters.read: A cost accounting textbook's chapters on job-order costing, process costing with equivalent units, and absorption versus variable costing, then SAP Learning material on product cost planning (BOM, routing, cost estimate).
chapters.produce: Cost one custom job and one month of a bottling process by hand, then write a half-page note on how SAP would get the same numbers from a BOM, routing and activity prices.

quiz.q: Which business is best suited to process costing rather than job costing?
opts: A consulting firm running client projects
A plant bottling a single soft drink in large volumes
quiz.ex: Process costing averages costs over many identical units; the others produce distinct jobs.

quiz.q: A job uses direct materials of ¥120,000 and 40 direct labour hours at ¥2,000 per hour. Overhead is applied at ¥1,500 per direct labour hour. What is the total job cost?
The firm prices jobs at cost plus a 30% markup on cost. What price is quoted for a job costing ¥260,000?
A process has no opening work in process. 5,000 units are started; 4,200 are completed; 800 remain 25% complete for conversion. How many equivalent units of conversion are there?
Same process: materials (added at the start) cost ¥1,000,000 and conversion costs are ¥1,056,000. 4,200 units were completed and 800 remain 25% converted. What is the cost of the completed units?
quiz.ex: Materials per unit 1,000,000 ÷ 5,000 = 200. Conversion per unit 1,056,000 ÷ 4,400 = 240. Completed 4,200 × 440 = 1,848,000.

quiz.q: Under absorption costing, fixed manufacturing overhead is:
opts: Included in product cost, so part of it sits in inventory until the goods are sold
Expensed in full in the period it is incurred
quiz.ex: Absorption costing assigns fixed production overhead to units; variable costing treats it as a period cost.

chapters.title: Standard costing and variance analysis
chapters.read: A cost accounting textbook's 標準原価計算 chapter: setting standards, material price and quantity variances, labour rate and efficiency variances, and who is responsible for each.
chapters.produce: Take one month of plan versus actual data for a product and write a variance report that splits the total cost variance into price/quantity and rate/efficiency, with a sentence on the likely cause of each.

quiz.q: Standard: 2 kg of material per unit at ¥500 per kg. Actual output 1,000 units used 2,100 kg bought at ¥480 per kg. What is the size of the material price variance (it is favourable)?
Same data: standard 2 kg per unit at ¥500 per kg; 1,000 units made using 2,100 kg. What is the size of the material quantity variance (it is adverse)?
quiz.ex: Standard quantity 2,000 kg. (2,100 − 2,000) × 500 = 50,000 adverse.

quiz.q: Standard: 0.5 labour hours per unit at ¥1,800 per hour. 1,000 units were made using 520 hours paid at ¥1,900 per hour. What is the size of the labour rate variance (it is adverse)?
Same labour data: standard 0.5 hours per unit at ¥1,800; 1,000 units used 520 hours. What is the size of the labour efficiency variance (it is adverse)?
quiz.ex: Standard hours 500. (520 − 500) × 1,800 = 36,000 adverse.

quiz.q: A favourable material price variance appears together with an adverse material quantity variance. What is the most likely single explanation?
opts: Cheaper, lower-quality material was bought and caused more waste
quiz.ex: Lower-grade material lowers the price paid but raises the quantity used, linking the two variances.

quiz.q: Who is usually responsible for the material quantity (usage) variance?
quiz.ex: Usage is controlled on the factory floor; the purchasing manager usually answers for the price variance.

chapters.title: Budgeting
chapters.read: A management accounting textbook's budgeting chapters: the master budget sequence (sales, production, materials, labour, overhead, cash), flexible budgets, and alternatives such as zero-based budgeting.
chapters.produce: Build a linked quarterly master budget in a spreadsheet for a small manufacturer, from sales budget through to a cash budget that flags months needing a bank loan.

quiz.q: Budgeted sales are 10,000 units. Desired closing finished goods are 1,500 units and opening finished goods are 1,200 units. How many units must be produced?
Production is 10,300 units, each needing 2 kg of material. Desired closing material stock is 3,000 kg and opening stock is 2,500 kg. How many kg must be purchased?
Credit sales are collected 60% in the month of sale and 40% in the following month. Sales were ¥1,000,000 in April and ¥1,500,000 in May. What are cash collections in May?
What is a flexible budget used for?
opts: Comparing actual costs with the budget adjusted to the actual level of output
Fixing all costs at the original plan regardless of output
quiz.ex: Flexing the budget to actual volume separates volume effects from spending efficiency.

quiz.q: What is the defining feature of zero-based budgeting?
opts: Last year's budget is rolled forward with an inflation uplift
Budgets are set to zero for loss-making units
Every activity must be justified from scratch each period
quiz.ex: Zero-based budgeting starts from nothing rather than from the previous year's figures.

quiz.q: Which budget is normally prepared first in a master budget?
quiz.ex: Sales volume drives production, purchasing, labour and cash, so it is the starting point.

chapters.title: Profitability analysis by segment
chapters.read: A management accounting textbook's chapter on segment reporting and the contribution approach (contribution margin, traceable fixed costs, segment margin), then SAP Learning material on margin analysis / CO-PA characteristics and value fields.
chapters.produce: Build a segment P&L for a company with three regions and two products, showing contribution margin and segment margin by cell, and write a short recommendation on which segment to fix or exit.

quiz.q:
Segment data:
East: sales ¥8,000,000; variable costs ¥4,800,000; traceable fixed costs ¥1,500,000
West: sales ¥5,000,000; variable costs ¥3,500,000; traceable fixed costs ¥1,800,000
Common fixed costs ¥1,000,000
What is East's contribution margin?

Same data:
West: sales ¥5,000,000; variable costs ¥3,500,000; traceable fixed costs ¥1,800,000
What is West's segment margin? (Enter a negative number for a loss.)
quiz.ex: Contribution 1,500,000 − traceable fixed 1,800,000 = −300,000.

quiz.q: Same data: West has a segment margin of −¥300,000. If West is closed, all its traceable fixed costs disappear and common fixed costs are unchanged. What happens to company profit?
quiz.ex: The company loses West's 1,500,000 contribution but saves 1,800,000 of traceable fixed cost: a net gain of 300,000.

quiz.q:
Same data:
East: sales ¥8,000,000; variable ¥4,800,000; traceable fixed ¥1,500,000
West: sales ¥5,000,000; variable ¥3,500,000; traceable fixed ¥1,800,000
Common fixed costs ¥1,000,000
What is the company's operating profit?
quiz.ex: Segment margins: East 1,700,000, West −300,000, total 1,400,000. Less common 1,000,000 = 400,000.

quiz.q: Which statement about SAP profitability analysis (CO-PA) is correct?
opts: Account-based analysis uses G/L accounts and reconciles directly with FI, while costing-based analysis stores amounts in value fields
Costing-based analysis always reconciles exactly with FI
Account-based analysis cannot report by customer
Neither type can analyse contribution margin
quiz.ex: Account-based (margin analysis in S/4HANA) works on G/L accounts; costing-based uses its own value fields and can differ from FI.

quiz.q: In CO-PA, 'customer group' and 'region' are examples of:
quiz.ex: Characteristics are the dimensions you slice results by; value fields hold the amounts and quantities.

boss.q: A company sells products A and B in a fixed mix of 2 A for every 1 B. Contribution per unit: A ¥600, B ¥900. Fixed costs are ¥2,100,000. How many units in total (A plus B) must be sold to break even?
boss.ex: One mix package (2A + 1B) contributes 2 × 600 + 900 = 2,100. Packages needed 2,100,000 ÷ 2,100 = 1,000, i.e. 2,000 A + 1,000 B = 3,000 units.

boss.q: A company has total contribution of ¥1,200,000 and operating profit of ¥300,000. If sales volume rises by 10% (prices and cost structure unchanged), by what percentage does operating profit rise?
boss.ex: Degree of operating leverage = 1,200,000 ÷ 300,000 = 4. Profit rises 4 × 10% = 40% (check: contribution +120,000 on 300,000).

boss.q: Budgeted fixed overhead is ¥2,000,000 for 10,000 standard hours, so it is absorbed at ¥200 per hour. Actual output was worth 9,000 standard hours. What is the size of the fixed overhead volume variance (it is adverse)?
boss.ex: (10,000 − 9,000) × 200 = 200,000 adverse: 1,000 fewer hours absorbed than budgeted.

boss.q: Standard: 3 kg per unit at ¥300 per kg. 1,500 units were produced using 4,700 kg. 5,000 kg were bought for ¥1,550,000. What is the size of the material quantity variance (it is adverse)?
boss.ex: Standard quantity 4,500 kg. (4,700 − 4,500) × 300 = 60,000 adverse. The purchase price is irrelevant to the quantity variance.

boss.q: A new company produces 10,000 units and sells 9,000. Fixed manufacturing overhead is ¥1,500,000. There is no opening inventory. By how much does absorption costing profit exceed variable costing profit?
boss.ex: Fixed overhead per unit 150. 1,000 units in closing inventory carry 150,000 of fixed overhead that variable costing expenses immediately.

boss.q: A machine cost centre plans ¥6,000,000 for 4,000 hours. A production order consumes 12 machine hours and ¥30,000 of materials, and receives an overhead surcharge of 10% on materials. What is the total cost on the order?

Making a component costs ¥800 variable per unit plus ¥200 of allocated factory fixed cost that will not change either way. An outside supplier offers it at ¥900. What should the company do on cost grounds?
opts: Buy it, because the fixed cost will disappear
Buy it, because the full cost of ¥1,000 exceeds ¥900
Make it, because the relevant cost of making (¥800) is ¥100 below the purchase price
Be indifferent, because the costs are equal
boss.ex: Unavoidable fixed costs are irrelevant; comparing 800 with 900 favours making.

boss.q: Opening cash is ¥500,000. Budgeted collections are ¥1,300,000 and payments ¥1,450,000. The company must keep a minimum balance of ¥400,000. How much must it borrow?
boss.ex: Closing before borrowing = 500,000 + 1,300,000 − 1,450,000 = 350,000. Shortfall to the minimum = 400,000 − 350,000 = 50,000.

boss.q: A division has invested capital of ¥10,000,000 and operating profit of ¥1,500,000. The cost of capital is 10%. What is its residual income?
Why can allocating common fixed costs to segments mislead closure decisions?
opts: Common costs disappear when any segment closes
A segment with a positive segment margin can look loss-making, and closing it would reduce total profit
Contribution margin cannot be calculated once costs are allocated
boss.ex: Common costs stay after a closure, so only contribution and traceable fixed costs matter for the decision.
